entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4934"/><div sID="gen7258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4934"/><hi type="bold">6. The crimes alleged, on a harsh inference, by Eliphaz against Job are such as he would think likely to be committed by a rich man. The Mosaic law (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.26">Ex 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.10">De 24:10</reference>) subsequently embodied the feeling that existed among the godly in Job's time against oppression of debtors as to their pledges. Here the case is not quite the same; Job is charged with taking a pledge where he had no just claim to it; and in the second clause, that pledge (the outer garment which served the poor as a covering by day and a bed by night) is represented as taken from one who had not "changes of raiment" (a common constituent of wealth in the East), but was poorly clad--</hi>"naked" (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.36">Mt 25:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15">Jas 2:15</reference>); a sin the more heinous in a rich man like Job. <div eID="gen7258" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4947"/><div sID="gen7279" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4947"/>19. Triumph of the pious at the fall of the recent followers of the antediluvian sinners. While in the act of denying that God can do them any good or harm, they are cut off by Him. Eliphaz hereby justifies himself and the friends for their conduct to Job: not derision of the wretched, but joy at the vindication of God's ways (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.42">Psa 107:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">Re 15:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.16.7">16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1">19:1</reference>, 2). <div eID="gen7279" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 19. Triumph of the pious at the fall of the recent followers of the antediluvian sinners. While in the act of denying that God can do them any good or harm, they are cut off by Him. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4948"/><div sID="gen7280" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4948"/>20. The triumphant speech of the pious. If "substance" be retained, translate, rather as the Septuagint, "Has not their substance been taken away, and ... ?" But the Hebrew is rather, "Truly our adversary is cut down" [Gesenius]. The same opposition exists between the godly and ungodly seed as between the unfallen and restored Adam and Satan (adversary); this forms the groundwork of the book (<reference osisRef="Job.1.1-Job.2.13">Job 1:1-2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Ge 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen7280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remnant--</hi>all that "is left" of the sinner; repeated from <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">Job 20:26</reference>, which makes Umbreit's rendering "glory" (Margin), "excellency," less probable.<div eID="gen7281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire--</hi>alluding to Job (<reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.34">15:34</reference>; 18:15). First is mentioned destruction by water (<reference osisRef="Job.22.16">Job 22:16</reference>); here, by fire (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.5-2Pet.3.7">2Pe 3:5-7</reference>). <div eID="gen7282" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 20. The triumphant speech of the pious. If "substance" be retained, translate, rather as the Septuagint, "Has not their substance been taken away, and ... ?" But the Hebrew is rather, "Truly our adversary is cut down" [Gesenius]. The same opposition exists between the godly and ungodly seed as between the unfallen and restored Adam and Satan (adversary); this forms the groundwork of the book ( Job 1:1-2:13 ; Ge 3:15 ). remnant-- all that "is left" of the sinner; repeated from Job 20:26 , which makes Umbreit's rendering "glory" (Margin), "excellency," less probable. fire-- alluding to Job ( Job 1:16 ; 15:34 ; 18:15). First is mentioned destruction by water ( Job 22:16 ); here, by fire ( 2Pe 3:5-7 ).
entries.reader_content_plain: 20. The triumphant speech of the pious. If "substance" be retained, translate, rather as the Septuagint, "Has not their substance been taken away, and ... ?" But the Hebrew is rather, "Truly our adversary is cut down" [Gesenius]. The same opposition exists between the godly and ungodly seed as between the unfallen and restored Adam and Satan (adversary); this forms the groundwork of the book ( Job 1:1-2:13 ; Ge 3:15 ). remnant-- all that "is left" of the sinner; repeated from Job 20:26 , which makes Umbreit's rendering "glory" (Margin), "excellency," less probable. fire-- alluding to Job ( Job 1:16 ; 15:34 ; 18:15). First is mentioned destruction by water ( Job 22:16 ); here, by fire ( 2Pe 3:5-7 ).

Rather, When (thy ways; from <reference osisRef="Job.22.28">Job 22:28</reference>) are cast down (for a time), thou shalt (soon again have joyful cause to) say, There is lifting up (prosperity returns back to me) [Maurer].<div eID="gen7302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>God.<div eID="gen7303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">humble--</hi>Hebrew, "him that is of low eyes." Eliphaz implies that Job is not so now in his affliction; therefore it continues: with this he contrasts the blessed effect of being humble under it (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.6">Jas 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5">1Pe 5:5</reference> probably quote this passage). Therefore it is better, I think, to take the first clause as referred to by "God resisteth the proud." When (men) are cast down, thou shalt say (behold the effects of) pride. Eliphaz hereby justifies himself for attributing Job's calamities to his pride. "Giveth grace to the humble," answers to the second clause. <div eID="gen7304" type="x-p"/>

But the Hebrew expresses the negative (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.21">1Sa 4:21</reference>); translate "Thus He (God) shall deliver him who was not guiltless," namely, one, who like Job himself on conversion shall be saved, but not because he was, as Job so constantly affirms of himself, guiltless, but because he humbles himself (<reference osisRef="Job.22.29">Job 22:29</reference>); an oblique attack on Job, even to the last.<div eID="gen7305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it--</hi>Rather, "he (the one not heretofore guiltless) shall be delivered through the purity (acquired since conversion) of thy hands"; by thy intercession (as <reference osisRef="Gen.18.26">Ge 18:26</reference>, &c.). [Maurer]. The irony is strikingly exhibited in Eliphaz unconsciously uttering words which exactly answer to what happened at last: he and the other two were "delivered" by God accepting the intercession of Job for them (<reference osisRef="Job.42.7">Job 42:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.42.8">8</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.22"/>
